guides.title: What to do when
guides.html:
Dated from late October 2026 for a Summer 2027 cycle.

The shape of the problem: sixteen deadlines are now confirmed on the programs' own pages, the wall lands between 9 January and 15 February 2027, and the rest of the 2027 pages are still unposted. So the work splits cleanly into build the reusable assets now and apply in a burst in January.

The earliest confirmed deadlines are MD Anderson CATALYST on 13 January and Yale Child Study on 14 January — three weeks before the February cluster, and easy to miss.

Now → 15 November: build the assets

Nothing here is program-specific. All of it gets reused twenty times.

  • CV. Two hours. Skeleton.
  • Master personal statement. The big one — 4–6 hours across a few sittings. Template.
  • Ask for letters. Two recommenders, by mid-November. Email template. This is the single most time-sensitive item, because it depends on someone else.
  • Apply to the three already open: Johns Hopkins Pathway SIP, Cincinnati Children's SURF, and INSPIRE at Indiana (2027 round was due to open in October). Doing one application end-to-end now makes the January batch far faster.
  • Decide the honest answer to "MD, PhD, or MD-PhD?" It changes which programs are worth applying to. Amgen, SUIP, MSRP and BioMedRAP are PhD-pipeline programs.

15 November → 15 December: open the gates

Most 2027 applications open in this window.

  • NIH SIP opens ~mid-November. Biggest single opportunity on the list — one application, hundreds of labs. Do it the week it opens.
  • Amgen Scholars opens 1 November. Pick 3–5 host campuses. The essays overlap heavily, so each extra host costs maybe 40 minutes.
  • Leadership Alliance opens 1 November. One application, many institutions.
  • Jackson Lab opens in November, deadline confirmed 25 January, 5pm ET.
  • St. Jude POE opened 1 November, deadline 1 February — and that deadline covers letters too. They advise getting credentials in by mid-to-late December.
  • Cold-email PIs. Three or four per program you seriously want. Template. Do this before the application, so you can name a mentor who has already said yes.
  • 1 December: Seattle Children's, Children's Colorado and Yale Child Study open. Weill Cornell opens 8 December.

15 December → 9 January: the first wall

  • 2 January: Seattle Children's deadline (projected), Rutgers RWJMS opens.
  • 9 January: Fred Hutch SURP — rising seniors only, so this is the year it is available to you.
  • 11 January: Broad Institute BSRP (projected).
  • 13 January: MD Anderson CATALYST — CONFIRMED. Opens 16 November, so there is plenty of runway if you start it in the November block.
  • 14 January: Yale Child Study, 5pm ET — CONFIRMED. The first confirmed deadline of the cycle and the easiest to lose track of.
  • 15 January: Cold Spring Harbor URP (projected), INSPIRE, MIT MSRP.
  • 16 January: earliest Vanderbilt VSSA track closes — the tracks close on different dates through 15 February, so check yours specifically.

Holidays eat this window. Anything not drafted by 20 December gets done badly.

9 January → 15 February: the main burst

Most of the list is due here, clustered hard on 1 February.

  • 23 January: Boston Children's epilepsy internship opens; Newborn Medicine deadline.
  • 25 January: Jackson Lab, 5pm ET — CONFIRMED.
  • 31 January: Penn State PROMISE — CONFIRMED.
  • 1 February: the big cluster, all confirmed: St. Jude POE, Amgen Scholars (all US hosts), Penn State SURIP, UCSF SRTP, MSK MBSP — note the 8:00 a.m. cutoff, not end of day, Stanford SSRP, and most Vanderbilt tracks. Plus CHOP CRISSP, Hopkins and Penn SUIP (projected).
  • 2 February: NYU SURP, 5pm — CONFIRMED.
  • 3 February: Leadership Alliance and Mayo SURF — CONFIRMED. Note both are the 3rd, not the 1st. The Leadership Alliance deadline covers the whole package, letters and official transcripts included.
  • 7 February: Nationwide Children's (projected).
  • 13 February: ECU Brody SBRP (projected — 2027 cycle opens 2 November).
  • 15 February: Penn State AHA-USF (confirmed), latest Vanderbilt tracks, NIH SIP (projected), NSF REU sites.
  • 22 February: Caltech SURF (projected). Different from everything else here — the application IS a research proposal written with a prospective mentor, so contact has to happen weeks earlier. Start it in January.

Do not leave 1 February to the last week. Thirty applications sharing one deadline is the single biggest failure mode in this cycle. Work backwards: a third of them done by 20 January, two-thirds by 27 January.

15 February → March: insurance

  • 15 March: NYSCF Summer Research Internship — confirmed, and genuinely late. Worth keeping in reserve.
  • Sweep Pathways to Science and the NSF REU portal for programs with March and April deadlines.
  • Email the NIA Alzheimer's centers directly — those placements are arranged, not advertised, and they run on a different clock.

March → April: decisions

Most programs decide between late March and mid-April. Amgen notifies by end of March; St. Jude by around 1 April.

If nothing lands: the ADRC route, direct PI emails, and your own university's summer research funding are all still live in April. A summer in a home-campus lab with a real project is worth more than a prestigious program you did not get.

The honest summary

Three things decide this cycle, in order:

  1. Letters requested by mid-November. The only item gated on someone else.
  2. Cold emails to PIs. Fifteen minutes each, and the only lever that moves the odds at a specific institution.
  3. Not cramming 1 February. Spread that cluster across two weeks.

Everything else is execution.

guides.title: How to get picked
guides.html:
Useful context for where to spend effort. None of this is a secret — it is just not written down anywhere an applicant naturally looks.

Who reads the application

For a large program (NIH SIP, CHOP, St. Jude), it is usually two stages:

  1. A screen against hard criteria: eligibility, citizenship, class year, GPA floor, completeness. This stage is mechanical. Most rejections happen here and have nothing to do with how good the applicant is.
  2. Faculty review. Files get routed to labs by research area. A PI scans for: does this person want to do what we do, and can they be useful for ten weeks?

The second stage is the one worth optimising for, and it hinges on specificity.

What the screen is checking

Every one of these is in the dataset, and failing any of them wastes the whole application:

  • Citizenship. NSF REUs, NIH SIP, Amgen and many others require US citizen or permanent resident. No exceptions, no appeals. Filter on this first.
  • Class year. Fred Hutch takes rising seniors only. Many programs exclude students who graduate before or during the summer. Seattle Children's excludes anyone graduating during the program.
  • GPA floor. St. Jude wants 3.40 in math/science and overall. Amgen wants 3.2. These are hard filters.
  • Availability for the full term. St. Jude requires one of four specific start dates and rejects applicants who cannot make one. The Broad requires all nine weeks. If you have a conflict, address it before applying, not after.
  • Completeness. Letters that arrive after the deadline sink otherwise strong applications. St. Jude's deadline covers credentials too.

The site's filters exist mostly to stop you spending four hours on a program you are not eligible for.

What the faculty review is weighing

Roughly in order:

  1. Fit with a specific lab. The single biggest factor, and the one most within your control. An application that names a PI, references their work, and says why, lands in a different pile. If you have emailed that PI and they said yes, it is a different pile again.
  2. Evidence of follow-through. Ten weeks is short. They are looking for signs someone will not need babysitting: a project you ran, a protocol you handled, a semester of consistent lab hours, a job that required showing up.
  3. A real reason for the area. Not passion — a question. "I want to understand why seizure burden predicts developmental outcome" tells a reader where to route the file.
  4. Letters. Mostly used as corroboration. A detailed letter from someone who supervised you beats a glowing one from someone who taught you in a lecture.
  5. Grades and coursework. Matter at the screen, matter less here, as long as the relevant courses are there.

What does not move the needle

  • Enthusiasm as such. Everyone is enthusiastic.
  • Volume of extracurriculars unrelated to research or clinical work.
  • Prestige-signalling about the program in the essay. They know it is good.
  • A longer personal statement. Over-length is a mild negative.

The three asymmetries worth exploiting

One application, many labs. NIH SIP, Amgen Scholars, the Leadership Alliance and Vanderbilt's VSSA each put a single essay in front of many institutions or many labs. The marginal cost of the second, third and fifth is small. These should be done first and done well.

Cold emails. Fifteen minutes, and the only thing that converts an anonymous file into a named candidate. Most applicants never send one. Template.

Less-famous places with real research. Arkansas Children's, Stowers, Van Andel, UAB, Einstein, Nemours and Benaroya do genuine work and receive a fraction of the applications that CHOP and St. Jude get. A summer with a real project and a mentor who had time beats a rejection from a famous program. Build the list with a few of these in it deliberately.

On the thin-experience problem

If your research experience is light, that is the normal state for a rising junior and several programs are built for it — Seattle Children's explicitly prioritises first-time research interns, and NSF REUs are designed as entry points.

What helps: a serious course project described as research, specific technical skills you can actually perform, and a letter from someone who has watched you work. What does not help: apologising for it in the personal statement.

A realistic expectation

These programs run acceptance rates in the low single digits to low teens. Strong applicants get rejected from most places they apply. The right response is volume on the reusable applications plus a handful of genuinely attainable targets — not six perfect applications to six famous programs.

Twelve to twenty applications is a reasonable target for this cycle, and the structure in this repo is built to make that a realistic amount of work rather than an impossible one.

guides.title: Reading a program page
guides.html:
Program pages bury the things that decide whether an application is worth starting. This is the order to look for them.

The five disqualifiers — check these first

Before reading a single word about the research, find:

  1. Citizenship requirement. "US citizen or permanent resident" appears on most federally funded programs. Non-negotiable.
  2. Class year. Look for "rising senior", "must have completed sophomore year", "may not graduate before/during the program". Fred Hutch and Seattle Children's both have hard rules here that point in opposite directions.
  3. GPA minimum. Often in a FAQ rather than the main page.
  4. Dates. Fixed start dates (St. Jude has four and only four), and whether the full term is mandatory.
  5. Deadline, and what it covers. Specifically: are letters due on the same date, or later? St. Jude's deadline includes credentials. The Broad gave letters two extra days.

If any of these rule you out, stop. That is a win — four hours saved.

Then find the mentor list

The most valuable page on any program site, and often two clicks deep: "Faculty", "Mentors", "Research areas", "Labs", or a PDF of last year's projects.

This is where the why-this-program paragraph and the cold emails come from. A program with no published mentor list is one where naming a mentor matters less — and a program with a long list is one where naming a mentor matters a great deal.

Then the practicalities

  • Stipend — and whether housing is separate. A $7,500 stipend with housing included (Jackson Lab) is worth far more than $5,000 with no housing in Boston.
  • Housing — provided, subsidised, or your problem.
  • Travel — Jackson Lab and several others reimburse it; most do not.
  • Length — nine to eleven weeks, and whether it collides with anything.

The dataset already has all of this, but verify it on the page before applying — the stipend figures in particular are the fields most likely to be stale.

Signs the page is from a previous cycle

Important right now, because most 2027 pages have not been updated:

  • Dates in 2025 or 2026 with no mention of 2027
  • "Applications are closed", "check back in the fall", "will open in November"
  • A deadline that has already passed

None of these mean the program is gone. They mean the new cycle is not posted. Note the date, and let the watcher catch the update:

python scripts/watch.py

It flags any page that changes, and specifically any page that starts mentioning 2027 — which is almost always the week the new cycle goes live.

When the page says almost nothing

Some real programs have one thin paragraph and an email address. That is not a bad sign — it often means placements are arranged directly rather than through a portal, which is good news for anyone willing to write an email.

In that case skip the application entirely and go straight to a cold email to the listed contact or to a relevant PI. The NIA Alzheimer's centers, UCSF pediatrics and the UC Davis MIND Institute all work this way.

guides.title: Personal statement
guides.html:
Write this once, properly. Then every application becomes: paste the master, swap the program-specific paragraph, adjust length. That is the difference between applying to six programs and applying to twenty.

Target length: 600–800 words. Most programs ask for 500–1000, and a tight 650 reads better than a padded 950.

The shape

Paragraph 1 — the specific thing that got you here (100–150 words)

Not "I have always loved science." One concrete moment, experience or question, and what it made you want to find out. If there is a personal reason behind the pediatric interest, this is where it goes — stated plainly, once, without reaching for drama.

Weak: "Ever since I was young, I have been fascinated by the human brain."

Better: "[CONCRETE MOMENT]. What stuck with me was not [the obvious part] but [the specific thing you noticed]. I wanted to know [the actual question]."

Paragraph 2 — what you have actually done (150–200 words)

Research experience, coursework that genuinely matters, lab skills, clinical or volunteer work. For each thing: what the question was, what you did, and what you learned about doing research — not just what the project was about.

Committees read for evidence that someone can be trusted with ten weeks of a mentor's time. Signals that help: you ran something independently, you handled a protocol, you dealt with a result that did not work.

"In [COURSE/LAB], I [SPECIFIC TASK — the assay, the dataset, the protocol]. [WHAT WENT WRONG OR SURPRISED YOU]. That taught me [SOMETHING REAL ABOUT RESEARCH, not a platitude]."

If you have little or no formal research experience: say so without apology and lean on transferable evidence — a hard course with a project component, a data analysis you did, a job that required precision and follow-through. Several programs on this list (Seattle Children's especially) explicitly prioritise students without prior research experience.

Paragraph 3 — what you want to work on (120–180 words)

The research area, and why. Be specific enough that a reader could guess which labs to route the application to. "Pediatric neurology, particularly how seizure burden affects development" is useful. "Biomedical research" is not.

Naming a method or model system helps: EEG, mouse models, patient-registry data, imaging, single-cell work.

Paragraph 4 — why this program, specifically (100–150 words)

The one paragraph that changes every time. See why-this-program.md. Never send an application where this paragraph could have been addressed to any other institution.

Paragraph 5 — where this goes (80–120 words)

MD, PhD, MD-PhD, or honestly undecided between them — all fine. What is not fine is vagueness that reads as not having thought about it. If undecided, say what the summer would help you decide.

Note: Amgen Scholars, SUIP, MSRP and BioMedRAP are explicitly PhD-pipeline programs. If you are aiming MD-only, those are a weaker fit than the hospital-based programs, and the statement should not pretend otherwise.

Before sending, check

  • Could this paragraph have been written by any other applicant? Rewrite it.
  • Does the program name appear, spelled correctly, in paragraph 4?
  • Is there at least one specific paper, lab or faculty member named?
  • Any sentence beginning "I am passionate about"? Delete it.
  • Read aloud — anywhere you stumble, a reader will too.
  • Within the word limit. Over-length gets cut or counted against.
  • Someone else proofread it. Not spellcheck — a person.

Three openings that work

  1. The question. Open with the thing you genuinely want to know, then how you came to care about it.
  2. The moment. A specific scene — in a lab, a clinic, a classroom — and the question it raised. Earns its place only if it leads somewhere.
  3. The problem. Something unresolved in the field, and where you want to stand in relation to it. Strongest option if you have read real literature; risky if you have not.

Avoid: quotations from famous scientists, dictionary definitions, "webster's defines", and childhood-illness framing unless it is genuinely yours to tell.

guides.title: CV skeleton
guides.html:
One page. Two only if there is genuinely a second page of content, which at this stage there usually is not.

A research CV is not a job resume. Drop the objective statement, drop "Microsoft Office", and lead with education and research.

[FULL NAME]
[email] · [phone] · [city, state] · [LinkedIn or ORCID, if either exists]


EDUCATION

[University]                                                  [City, State]
B.S. in [Major], expected [Month Year]                        GPA: [X.XX / 4.00]
  Minor in [X]
  Relevant coursework: [4–6 courses that matter — biochem, neuroscience,
  statistics, organic chemistry, research methods. Not intro bio.]
  [Honors, dean's list, scholarships]


RESEARCH EXPERIENCE

[Lab or Project Name], [Institution]                          [Month Year–present]
Supervisor: [Dr. Name]
  · [What the lab studies, in one line of plain English.]
  · [What YOU did — the technique, the assay, the dataset, the protocol.
     Start with a verb. "Performed," "Analyzed," "Maintained," "Coded."]
  · [A result, output or responsibility: a poster, a presentation, a dataset
     you owned, a protocol you ran unsupervised.]

[Course-based research, independent project, or honors thesis also goes here.
A serious semester project counts as research experience. Say what the question
was and what you did.]


CLINICAL & VOLUNTEER EXPERIENCE

[Role], [Organization]                                        [Month Year–Month Year]
  · [What you did and roughly how many hours.]
  · [Anything involving responsibility, patients, or data.]


TECHNICAL SKILLS

Laboratory: [PCR, cell culture, Western blot, immunohistochemistry, microscopy —
             only things you could do unsupervised tomorrow]
Data:       [R, Python, SPSS, Excel, REDCap, GraphPad Prism]
Other:      [Spanish (conversational), CITI human-subjects certification,
             IRB protocol experience]


PRESENTATIONS & PUBLICATIONS
[Only if real. Poster at a campus symposium counts and should be listed.]

[Last, F.] et al. "[Title]." [Venue], [Year]. [Poster / oral presentation]


AWARDS & HONORS

[Award], [Granting body]                                                 [Year]

Rules that matter

  • Reverse chronological within every section.
  • No pronouns. "Performed immunostaining," not "I performed immunostaining."
  • Verbs first. Not "Was responsible for maintaining cell cultures" but "Maintained cell cultures."
  • Be specific about skills. "Proficient in laboratory techniques" says nothing. "Mouse colony management, genotyping by PCR" says a lot.
  • Quantify where it is honest. "Enrolled 40 patients," "analysed 12 months of registry data."
  • One page, 10–11pt, generous margins. A cramped two-pager reads worse than a clean one-pager.
  • Export to PDF, named Lastname-Firstname-CV.pdf. Never send a .docx.

If the research section is thin

Normal for a rising junior, and not disqualifying — Seattle Children's explicitly prioritises first-time research interns, and plenty of others take students with no bench experience at all.

What to do: promote a serious course project into the research section with its real question and method. List coursework that signals readiness (statistics, biochem, a lab-heavy course). Put technical skills higher so they are seen early. Do not pad with high-school material.

guides.title: Asking for letters
guides.html:
Most programs on this list want two letters. The same two letters go everywhere, so this is a one-time cost — but only if you ask early and make it easy.

Ask by the end of November. Faculty write letters in batches, and the December–January window is when every pre-med in the country is asking.

Who to ask

In order of usefulness:

  1. A research mentor — anyone who has seen you work in a lab, even briefly. Nothing else is as persuasive.
  2. A professor from a small, hard course where you spoke up and did well. A seminar or lab course beats a 400-person lecture every time.
  3. A clinical or volunteer supervisor, if the program is clinically oriented.

Avoid: a famous professor who cannot pick you out of a crowd. A detailed letter from a postdoc beats a vague one from a department chair.

The email

Subject: Letter of recommendation — summer research applications (due early February)

Dear Professor [NAME],

I am applying to summer 2027 undergraduate research programs in [AREA], and I am hoping you would be willing to write me a letter of recommendation.

I took [COURSE] with you in [TERM] and [SPECIFIC THING — the project you did, something you contributed, the grade if it is good]. [IF A RESEARCH MENTOR: what you worked on and what you handled independently.]

Most deadlines fall between 9 January and 15 February 2027, and most programs collect letters through an online form that emails you a link directly. I have attached:

- my CV - my draft personal statement - a list of the programs and their deadlines - a short note on what I have been doing since your course

Would you be willing? If you do not feel you could write a strong letter, I would completely understand — I would rather know now.

Thank you for considering it.

[NAME]

That last paragraph matters. It gives a lukewarm writer a graceful exit, which is far better than a tepid letter you never see.

The packet to attach

Everything that makes writing easier makes the letter better:

  1. CV — current.
  2. Personal statement — the draft is fine. It tells them the story to corroborate.
  3. Program list with deadlines — export the CSV from the site, or send the site link.
  4. A reminder of who you are — a short paragraph: the course, the term, what you did well, anything memorable. Professors teach hundreds of students a year and this is a kindness, not an imposition.
  5. What to emphasise — if a program wants independence, say so.

Managing it afterwards

  • Log each recommender and each program in the tracker's notes field.
  • Most portals email the recommender a link only after you submit your part. Submit early so they have runway. St. Jude explicitly says to submit without waiting for letters.
  • Send a reminder ten days before the deadline if the portal still shows the letter as outstanding. Polite, short, with the link.
  • Thank them afterwards, and tell them the outcome either way. They are going to be asked again for medical school.

The honest timing note

A letter requested on 20 January for a 1 February deadline will be written in a hurry and will read like it. The same professor asked on 20 November writes a better letter for the same student. The quality difference is entirely in the lead time.

guides.title: Emailing a lab
guides.html:
The highest-return thing in this whole repo, and almost nobody does it.

Many summer programs ask applicants to name preferred mentors, and a fair number of placements come down to a faculty member saying "I would take this student." Several entries on this list — the Boston Children's epilepsy lab, the UC Davis MIND Institute, the NIA Alzheimer's centers, UCSF pediatrics — are effectively only reachable this way.

A good cold email takes fifteen minutes. Send three or four per program you seriously want.

The rules

  1. Short. Under 200 words. They are reading it on a phone between meetings.
  2. Specific. Name one of their papers and say something true about it. Generic praise is worse than none.
  3. Ask for one thing. Not "please mentor me for the summer" — just whether they are taking a summer student.
  4. Attach the CV. One PDF, named Lastname-Firstname-CV.pdf.
  5. Subject line that survives a crowded inbox.
  6. No follow-up for ten days. Then exactly one, and never a third.

Template

Subject: Summer 2027 research — undergraduate interested in [THEIR TOPIC]

Dear Dr. [LAST NAME],

I am a [YEAR] at [SCHOOL] studying [MAJOR], and I am applying to [PROGRAM NAME] for summer 2027. I am writing because I would like to work in your lab.

I read your [YEAR] paper on [SPECIFIC TOPIC — the actual finding, not the title]. [ONE SENTENCE THAT SHOWS YOU READ IT: something that surprised you, a question it raised, how it connects to what you want to understand.]

My background: [ONE SENTENCE — relevant coursework, lab experience, technique]. [IF APPLICABLE: a sentence on what you can already do that is useful — cell culture, R or Python, data entry on a clinical study.]

Are you taking a summer student in 2027? If the program application should name a preferred mentor, I would like to name you — but only if that would be welcome.

My CV is attached. Thank you for your time.

[FULL NAME] [SCHOOL], Class of [YEAR] [EMAIL] · [PHONE]

Finding the right PI

  1. Open the program page, find the faculty or mentor list.
  2. No list? Search the department site for the research area.
  3. Open two or three recent papers from each candidate on PubMed. If the abstracts bore you, you have saved yourself a summer.
  4. Check they are actually active — a lab whose last paper was 2019 may be winding down.
  5. Get the email from the faculty page, not from a paper's corresponding-author line, which is often stale.

What a reply looks like

  • "Yes, name me" — excellent. Put it in the application immediately and say so explicitly: "Dr. X has agreed to host me." That line is worth a lot.
  • "I am not taking students but talk to Dr. Y" — a warm introduction. Use it.
  • "Apply through the central program" — neutral, but you are now a name they have seen rather than one of 400 files.
  • Silence — the normal outcome. Not personal. Send more.

Worth knowing

Expect most emails to go unanswered. Ten emails producing one "yes" is a good rate, and that one yes can decide the summer. The failure mode is not sending them at all.

guides.title: Why this program
guides.html:
The only part of the application that cannot be reused — which is exactly why it carries so much weight. A committee can tell in one sentence whether an applicant looked at their page for ninety seconds or for twenty minutes.

Budget 20–30 minutes per program. That is the whole cost.

What goes in it

Three things, in roughly 100–150 words:

  1. Something only true of this program. A named faculty member, a center, a specific resource, the structure of the summer.
  2. Why that matches what you want to do. The connection stated explicitly — do not make the reader infer it.
  3. What you would bring. One line, concrete.

The research, in four steps

  1. Open the program page. Find the faculty or mentor list — this is the part worth the time.
  2. Pick two or three names whose work genuinely interests you.
  3. Look up one recent paper from each on PubMed. Read the abstract properly and skim the figures.
  4. Write the paragraph naming one or two of them and what specifically draws you.

A worked example

Vague — could be sent anywhere:

I am excited to apply to your program because of its strong reputation in pediatric research and the excellent mentorship it provides. I believe this program would help me grow as a researcher and prepare me for medical school.

Specific — could only be sent to this program:

I am applying to CRISSP because of the breadth of pediatric neurology work at CHOP, and Dr. [NAME]'s group in particular. Their 2025 paper on [TOPIC] found [SPECIFIC FINDING], which surprised me because [HONEST REACTION]. I have been trying to understand [RELATED QUESTION] since [YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE], and CHOP has the patient volume to ask it properly. I would come in able to [CONCRETE SKILL], and I am most interested in the [SPECIFIC METHOD] side of the work.

The second version is not better writing. It is better research.

Per-program angles for the top picks

Pulled from the dataset — use these as the starting point:

ProgramThe thing to name
NIH SIPName the institute (NICHD for pediatrics, NINDS for neuro, NIA for Alzheimer's) and a specific intramural lab. The application routes by institute.
Amgen ScholarsEach host is a separate application — the paragraph must be about that campus, not about Amgen.
Jackson LaboratoryThe independent-project structure and the written report. They care that applicants want to own a project.
Fred Hutch SURPRising-seniors-only. Say explicitly that this is your last summer before applying onward, and what you want to settle.
Leadership AllianceName preferred host institutions and why. The end-of-summer national symposium is a real draw — mention presenting.
St. Jude POEPediatric oncology specifically. They want people who want this, not generic biomedical research.
Vanderbilt VSSAName the sub-track (neuroscience, cancer biology, immunology) rather than the umbrella.
Boston Children's epilepsy labA single lab — the paragraph is effectively a cold email. Name Dr. Loddenkemper's work directly.
CHOP CRISSPEnormous institution; naming a division and a faculty member is what separates applications.
Seattle Children'sThey prioritise first-time research interns. If your experience is thin, that is an argument for you here — make it.

Check before sending

  • Program name spelled correctly, and it is the right program
  • At least one faculty member or center named
  • At least one specific paper, finding, or resource referenced
  • No sentence that would survive a find-and-replace of the institution name
  • The "what I bring" line is concrete, not a feeling

guides.title: How to use all this
guides.html:
Everything in here is a starting point, not a finished document. The parts in [SQUARE BRACKETS] are the parts only you can fill in — and they are the only parts a reader actually cares about.

The one idea worth internalising

Almost every applicant writes some version of "I have always been passionate about helping children and I am eager to learn." Selection committees read hundreds of those. They are not evidence of anything.

What gets someone selected is specificity: a particular question you find interesting, a particular reason this lab can answer it, and some evidence you can be useful in a lab for ten weeks. One concrete sentence about a paper you read beats three paragraphs of enthusiasm.

What to build, in order

#ThingTimeReuse
1CV2 hours onceEvery application
2Master personal statement4–6 hours once~80% reusable
3Recommendation requests30 min per recommenderSame letter goes everywhere
4Per-program paragraph20–30 min eachNever reusable — this is the point
5Cold emails to PIs15 min eachHighest leverage, lowest effort

Guides worth reading before writing:

  • How to actually get picked — what these committees weigh
  • The timeline — what to do between now and February
  • Reading a program page — finding the real requirements fast

The highest-leverage thing on this whole list

Cold-emailing PIs. Most programs let applicants name a preferred mentor, and many placements are effectively decided by whether a specific faculty member said "I would take this student." A short, specific email to three or four PIs per program moves the odds more than another round of polishing the personal statement. Template here.
